# Kuṭidūsakajātaka (Ja 321)

**ID:** Ja 321
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kuṭidūsakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** One Who Ruined a Hut
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja321
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kuṭidūsakajātaka* (Ja 321) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. The framing story records that the Buddha related it while staying at Jetavana concerning an unruly young disciple who burned down the leaf hut of the elder Mahākassapa near Rājagaha after the elder reprimanded him for deceit and improper behavior [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921; Rahula 1956; Fausböll 1883]. To demonstrate that this disciple had acted destructively out of resentment in a previous existence as well, the Buddha recounted a tale of the past involving a monkey and a *siṅgila* bird [Burlingame 1921]. When the bird reproved the shivering monkey for lacking a shelter despite possessing human-like hands and feet, the resentful monkey wrecked the bird's nest [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1883]. At the close of the story, the Buddha identified the monkey as the hut-burning pupil and the *siṅgila* bird as himself [Fausböll 1883] (though an English summary of the Dhammapada commentary identifies the bird as Kassapa) [Burlingame 1921].

Scholars cite the jātaka in discussions of early Buddhist monastic life, illustrating Mahākassapa's role in reproving laxity among junior monks and the friction that sometimes arose [Sarao and Long 2017; Rahula 1956]. In the Pali commentarial collection edited by Fausböll, the text heads the *Kuṭidūsakavagga* [Fausböll 1883].

DharmaNexus identifies no cross-language matches scoring 10 or above [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus detects 11 text-reuse matches, showing extensive textual sharing with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* (notably across segments §2.4–4.3) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§2.4–4.3 ↔ §561–567); Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0502a) (§2.4–4.3 ↔ §1326–1330)
